fetched_contents.text: Identifying Best Practices for Increasing HIV Pre-exposure Prophylaxis (PrEP) Use and Persistence in the United States: a Systematic Review . Author manuscript; available in PMC: 2024 Jul 1. Published in final edited form as: AIDS Behav. 2024 May 14;28(7):2340–2349. doi: 10.1007/s10461-024-04332-z Abstract A qualitative systematic review was conducted to evaluate pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) interventions, describe characteristics of best practices for increasing PrEP use and persistence, and explore research gaps based on current PrEP interventions. We searched CDC’s Prevention Research Synthesis (PRS) Project’s cumulative HIV database (includes CINAHL, EMBASE, Global Health, MEDLINE, PsycInfo, and Sociological Abstracts) to identify PrEP intervention studies conducted in the U.S., published between 2000 and 2022 (last searched January 2023). Eligibility criteria include studies that evaluated PrEP interventions for persons testing negative for HIV infection, or for healthcare providers who prescribed PrEP; included comparisons between groups or pre/post; and reported at least one relevant PrEP outcome. Each eligible intervention was evaluated on the quality of study design, implementation, analysis, and strength of evidence (PROSPERO registration number: CRD42021256460). Of the 26 eligible interventions, the majority were focused on men who have sex with men (n=18) and reported PrEP adherence outcomes (n = 12). Nine interventions met the criteria for Best Practices (i.e., evidence-based interventions, evidence-informed interventions). Five were digital health interventions while two implemented individual counseling, one offered motivational interviewing, and one provided integrated medical care with a PrEP peer navigator. Longer intervention periods may provide more time for intervention exposure to facilitate behavioral change, and engaging the community when developing, designing and implementing interventions may be key for effectiveness. For digital health interventions, two-way messaging may help participants feel supported. Research gaps included a lack of Best Practices for several populations (e.g., Black persons, Hispanic/Latino persons, persons who inject drugs, and women of color) and evidence for various intervention strategies (e.g., interventions for promoting provider’s PrEP prescription behavior, peer support). These findings call for more collaborative work with communities to develop interventions that work and implement and disseminate Best Practices for increasing PrEP use and persistence in communities. Keywords: HIV, Interventions, Systematic Review, Evidence-Based Practice, Pre-exposure Prophylaxis, PrEP User, PrEP Persistence Introduction Pre-exposure Prophylaxis (PrEP) taken as prescribed before HIV exposure is effective in preventing HIV infection among people exposed to HIV through sex or injection drug use [1]. The Ending the HIV Epidemic (EHE) initiative and the HIV National Strategic Plan 2021–2025 highlight PrEP as one of the key strategies to reduce new HIV infections [2,3]. It has been more than 10 years since the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved the first PrEP medication to prevent HIV transmission in 2012 [4]. Yet, there were still 36,136 HIV diagnoses in the U.S. in 2021; groups most affected are men (79%), gay, bisexual and other men who have sex with men (collectively referred to as MSM) (67%), Black/African American (hereafter referred to as Black) or Hispanic/Latino persons (59%), people aged 13 to 34 (56%), and those living in South (52%) [5]. Overall, PrEP prescriptions have been increasing among persons in the U.S. who could benefit, but still remain lower than the national goals [6,7]. Despite these increases, PrEP coverage is far from equal and substantial disparities persist among subgroups (e.g., Blacks and Hispanic/Latinos have lower rates of PrEP prescriptions than White persons). Identifying effective interventions for increasing PrEP use is important in reaching national HIV prevention goals. To inform national prevention efforts, the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention’s (CDC’s) Prevention Research Synthesis (PRS) Project [8] has conducted an on-going evaluation of PrEP interventions since 2020. The PRS Project has been identifying evidence-based interventions (EBIs) and evidence-informed (EIs), collectively referred to as Best Practices, for increasing PrEP use and persistence in its Compendium, a compilation of effective HIV interventions [9]. The purposes of this study are to 1) summarize the characteristics of Best Practices for increasing PrEP use and persistence in the U.S. and 2) explore the research gaps based in the current PrEP behavioral intervention literature. Methods A protocol was registered in PROSPERO (CRD42021256460) [10]. Our report followed the guidelines from the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-analysis (PRSIMA) Statement [11]. Systematic Search Strategy The PRS Project has an overarching goal to synthesize the published scientific research literature to help inform policy decisions, guidelines, programmatic efforts, and future research in HIV prevention. The project has built a cumulative database that supports synthesis of HIV intervention research. fetched_contents.text: A patient-centered, combination intervention to support adherence to HIV pre-exposure prophylaxis during pregnancy and breastfeeding: a randomized pilot study in Malawi . Author manuscript; available in PMC: 2025 Jan 1. Published in final edited form as: J Acquir Immune Defic Syndr. 2024 Jan 1;95(1):42–51. doi: 10.1097/QAI.0000000000003309 Abstract Background: Daily oral pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) can reduce HIV incidence in pregnant and breastfeeding women, but adherence is essential. Methods: We conducted a pilot randomized trial to evaluate an intervention package to enhance antenatal and postnatal PrEP use in Lilongwe, Malawi. The intervention was based on patient-centered counseling adapted from prior PrEP studies, with the option of a participant-selected adherence supporter. Participants were locally eligible for PrEP and randomized 1:1 to intervention or standard counseling (i.e., control) and followed for six months. Participants received the intervention package or standard counseling at enrollment, one month, three months, and six months. Adherence was measured via plasma and intracellular tenofovir concentrations and scored using a published algorithm. Our primary outcome was retention in care with concentrations consistent with 4–7 doses/week. Results: From June to November 2020, we enrolled 200 pregnant women with median gestational age of 26 (IQR:19–33) weeks. Study retention was high at three months (89.5%) and six months (85.5%). In contrast, across the two timepoints, 32.8% had adherence scores consistent with 2–5 doses/week and 10.3% had scores consistent with daily dosing. For the composite primary endpoint, no substantial differences were observed between the intervention and control groups at three months (28.3% vs. 29.0%, probability difference [PD]:−0.7%, 95%CI:−13.3%, 11.8%) or at six months (22.0% vs. 26.3%, PD:−4.3%, 95%CI:−16.1%, 7.6%). Conclusions: In this randomized trial of PrEP adherence support, retention was high, but less than one-third of participants had pharmacologically confirmed adherence of ≥4 doses/week. Future research should focus on antenatal and postnatal HIV prevention needs and their alignment across the PrEP continuum, including uptake, persistence, and adherence. fetched_contents.text: Experiences of Using a Digital Text Messaging Intervention to Support Oral Medication Adherence for People Living With Type 2 Diabetes: Qualitative Process Evaluation Abstract Background Poor adherence to oral medications for type 2 diabetes can increase the risk of health complications. Digital interventions can affect people’s experiences of self-managing a chronic condition, and SMS text messages may provide an effective delivery method for an intervention. The Support Through Mobile Messaging and Digital Health Technology for Diabetes (SuMMiT-D) intervention uses evidence-based SMS text messages to support people with type 2 diabetes with regular and consistent use of diabetes medication. Objective This process analysis, conducted alongside a randomized controlled trial of SuMMiT-D, aimed to explore (1) the contextual factors that may interact with the SuMMiT-D intervention and (2) the self-reported mechanisms through which change in behavior or attitude might occur. Methods A nested qualitative process study was conducted within primary care in England. A total of 43 trial participants diagnosed with type 2 diabetes were assigned to receive the SuMMiT-D intervention, were undergoing oral glucose-lowering treatment, blood pressure-lowering treatment or lipid-lowering treatment, either alone or in combination, and had access to a mobile phone, took part in semistructured telephone interviews. Data were analyzed using inductive thematic analysis. Results In total, 2 overarching themes were developed exploring relevant contextual factors and potential mechanisms of change. The system exerted a range of holistic benefits and supported the cognitions, beliefs, and behaviors necessary for longitudinal self-management. The perceived value of the messages was fluid and linked to contextual need. Appraisal of the system was influenced by existing routines, lifestyle disruption, people’s understanding of type 2 diabetes, relationships with other people, and subjective attitudes toward living with type 2 diabetes in contemporary society. Conclusions This work demonstrates the value of engaging people longitudinally in thinking about their general health, the importance of interrogating context, and the holistic benefit of health messaging. Many people perceived wide-ranging and unexpected benefits from using the intervention over time, challenging assumptions about who might be expected to appraise the system more positively and who should be offered access to it. According to the World Health Organization, the global prevalence of diabetes in 2014 was 8.5% [1]. In the United Kingdom, the number of people living with diabetes reached 5 million for the first time in 2023 [2], with approximately 90% living with a diagnosis of T2D. While lifestyle changes can help control T2D, many people will require medication to lower their glucose levels. Medication adherence is important to help lower the long-term risks of developing complications [3], and even small improvements in glycemic control are associated with a significant reduction in potentially debilitating long-term health complications. However, engagement with self-management is crucial for good glycemic control; people do not always take their medication as intended, and it has been reported that people who are prescribed self-administered medications typically take only approximately half their prescribed doses [4]. As such, there is growing interest in harnessing simple and ubiquitous technologies to deliver evidence-based interventions to address this challenge [6]. fetched_contents.text: Facilitators and Barriers to Hiv Pre-Exposure Prophylaxis Adherence and Retention Among Young Men Who have Sex With Men: A Meta-Ethnographic Scoping Review Show available content in Abstract Retention and adherence to daily oral pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) are critical for effective HIV prevention; however, YMSM exhibit lower rates of both compared to other populations. This is important because young men who have sex with men (YMSM) are at higher risk for HIV, and understanding their challenges can help create better support and interventions. This scoping review synthesizes evidence on the facilitators and barriers to HIV PrEP retention and adherence among YMSM, focusing on individuals aged 10 to 29 years. The review adheres to PRISMA-ScR and eMERGe guidelines, examining 14 studies involving 3,178 participants. It emphasizes the complex interactions of individual, interpersonal, community, and societal factors influencing PrEP adherence and retention. Key facilitators include psychological strategies, supportive health systems, and supportive social networks. Conversely, significant barriers encompass financial burdens, interpersonal stigma, and behavioral factors. The review highlights the critical role of tailored, multi-level interventions and the need for healthcare provider training in youth-specific approaches to care. This work contributes to a nuanced understanding of PrEP retention among YMSM, offering insights crucial for designing effective public health strategies to enhance prevention-effective PrEP utilization in this high-risk population. Keywords: Daily oral pre-exposure prophylaxis, Young men who have sex with men, Adherence, Retention in care Introduction Since being identified in the 1980s, HIV has been a significant global public health challenge, especially among men who have sex with men (MSM), who have been disproportionately affected by this disease [1–3]. In 2020, approximately 25% of new global HIV infections were among MSM [4]. In numerous contexts, the highest rates of HIV incidence are observed in younger MSM populations, who was widely defined as 24 years old or younger [5, 6]. One study in the United States (US) demonstrated that MSM aged 18–24 years face a 2.5 times higher risk of HIV acquisition compared to their older counterparts [7]. In Thailand, the incidence of HIV among MSM aged 18–21 years was reported at 8.8 per 100 person-years, versus 5.9 per 100 person-years across all MSM between 2006 and 2012 [8]. In the UK, the highest increases in new HIV diagnoses were among young MSM aged 15–24 years from 2003 to 2012 [9]. Without prompt public health response and proper intervention, the number of HIV infections among YMSM will likely continue to grow. Oral pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) is an HIV prevention method that reduces the risk of HIV acquisition through daily use or a 2 + 1 + 1 schedule, so-called event-driven PrEP, of an anti-HIV medication (tenofovir disoproxil fumarate/emtricitabine) [10–12]. The effectiveness of PrEP depends on both retention in PrEP care and adherence to the medication as prescribed [13]. High retention and adherence rates are associated with a significant reduction in HIV incidence, highlighting the importance of both factors in maximizing the preventive potential of PrEP. Studies have shown that individuals with suboptimal retention and adherence are more likely to acquire HIV than those who are retained in PrEP care and adherent to PrEP [14–16]. Because the daily oral PrEP was the first widely available regimen and globally used, our scoping review focus on daily oral PrEP. Additionally, different PrEP regimens might introduce different facilitators and barriers (e.g., injection-related pain or fear might be a barrier of CAB-LA but would not affect daily oral PrEP). While PrEP is an HIV preventive measure with proven effectiveness that can suppress the growing HIV epidemic among MSM, retention and adherence to PrEP among MSM are influenced by several factors. In addition to general obstacles, such as cost, stigma, relationship conflicts, and concern about side effects, YMSM face a lack of insurance, fear of disclosing their true sexual identity to parents, and financial instability [17]. Fear of being labeled as promiscuous or HIV-positive, concerns about confidentiality, and lack of knowledge about PrEP have also been identified as potential barriers to PrEP retention for YMSM [13]. Conversely, effective facilitators for PrEP adherence include an established daily routine, the use of PrEP reminders, and social support [18]. While the barriers and facilitators for PrEP adherence and retention among the MSM community have been extensively studied, available evidence on this topic among YMSM has yet to be synthesized. Current reviews have not shed light on the differences between MSM across age groups, and are thus unable to put forward specific recommendations for YMSM [13, 17]. YMSM are ofent highly active on dating apps or social platform where they find their male sex partners and they have limited health literacy [19, 20]. Given the rising prevalence of HIV among YMSM as well as the distinct characteristics of this population, it is of great importance to understand the factors and needs that may impact their ability to use and adhere to PrEP successfully. Therefore, we conducted a scoping review with a meta-synthesis of qualitative findings to synthesize barriers and facilitators related to PrEP retention and adherence among YMSM. Core retention strategies used by health services in PrEP studies were broad and often combined counseling, linkage to care, peer navigation, and reminder/remediation systems. The evidence suggests that counseling was central to routine care, with one review noting that clinicians should provide medication adherence counseling and behavioral risk reduction support in conjunction with HIV-related services [N1-R4]. A systematic review also found that among 26 eligible interventions, nine met Best Practices, including individual counseling, motivational interviewing, integrated medical care with a PrEP peer navigator, and digital health interventions [N1-F1]. In another setting, a patient-centered combination intervention included patient-centered counseling adapted from prior PrEP studies plus the option of a participant-selected adherence supporter [N3-F2]. These examples show that counseling was not a stand-alone gimmick but was integrated into service delivery and tailored to participants’ preferences.

Linkage to care was also a major strategy, especially for retention in the care cascade. The systematic review explicitly included linkage/retention/re-engagement in HIV care as one of the five topic areas in its cumulative database [N1-F1], and the abstract notes that linkage to PrEP care was among the most commonly reported outcomes [N1-R1]. In practice, services combined linkage with retention; for example, the PATH-PrEP study involved linkage to care and HIV/STI testing as part of a broader prevention package [N4-R3]. The evidence also points to peer navigation as a retained strategy: the systematic review cited integrated medical care with a PrEP peer navigator as one of the Best Practices [N1-F1], and another study emphasized the crucial role of PrEP navigators in facilitating access to HIV prevention services [N2-R2]. So peer navigation was used to support access and retention rather than being an afterthought.

Reminder systems were similarly embedded in routine care. The systematic review identified digital health interventions and noted that two-way messaging may help participants feel supported [N1-F1]. In a separate text-messaging intervention study, SMS was described as a low-cost approach to support medication adherence and lifestyle management, with messages designed to affect self-management and behavior change [N5-F3]. Though this is not a PrEP-specific study, its evidence base is directly relevant here because it illustrates how reminder-based digital support was used in health services. The evidence also indicates that services used follow-up visits and objective adherence testing to identify patients at risk of dropping out [N6-R4]. That is, health services did not rely on a single intervention; they used monitoring and remediation to keep people engaged.

Delivery models were varied and often mixed. Clinic-based delivery was clearly the baseline model, especially for integrated care and standard counseling [N1-F1][N3-F2]. Home-based delivery emerged as a separate model, with one study assessing the acceptability and feasibility of a home-based PrEP program [N7-R5]. Telehealth/telePrEP was another major model, with systematic reviews and reports describing virtual service delivery, telePrEP programs, and the effects of telePrEP on service delivery [N7-R1][N7-R3]. The evidence also points to hybrid models: the PATH-PrEP study combined behavioral and linkage-to-care components [N4-R3], and the Malawi pilot study was delivered through antenatal and postnatal platforms [N3-F2]. So delivery models were not fixed; they were adapted to the setting, and many studies used combinations of clinic visits, home-based support, and telehealth.

Whether strategies were integrated or stand-alone depended on the intervention design. Counseling and peer navigation were often integrated into routine care, such as in standard counseling and integrated medical care [N1-F1][N3-F2]. Digital interventions, by contrast, were sometimes stand-alone in their design, such as SMS-based interventions [N5-R2][N5-R5]. The review also emphasized that digital health interventions may be highly scalable, but the evidence base is still limited for some populations [N1-F1]. In short, the evidence supports a spectrum from routine clinic-based care with counseling and peer support, through home-based and telehealth models, to digital reminder systems and hybrid programs [N1-F1][N3-F2][N7-R1].

Digital and remote support strategies in the evidence were centered on text messaging, telehealth, and digital messaging systems. Text messaging was the most frequently cited tool, with studies describing SMS-based interventions, text-messaging applications, and ecological momentary intervention systems [N5-R1][N5-R3]. The evidence also explicitly links text messaging to medication adherence support and self-management [N5-F3]. In PrEP-specific studies, SMS text messaging improved adequate PrEP adherence among young MSM [N5-R5], and an interactive text-messaging intervention improved adherence among young MSM in Chicago [N5-R2]. The digital text messaging intervention was therefore used as a stand-alone support strategy to reinforce adherence and retention.

Telehealth/telePrEP was another major digital support model. The evidence includes a systematic review of telePrEP programs in the U.S., which aimed to describe model characteristics and summarize clinical, implementation, and equity outcomes [N7-R1][N7-R4]. A CDC report also evaluated the effect of telePrEP on delivery of PrEP services at the Denver Sexual Health Clinic [N7-R2]. These sources indicate that telehealth was used as a remote delivery model rather than a one-off tool, and that it was positioned as a scalable and flexible option for service delivery [N7-R1]. The evidence further suggests that telehealth can be leveraged in public health emergencies, such as during the pandemic, which reinforces its remote support function [N7-R3].

Retention outcomes measured in these studies included adherence and appointment attendance. Text messaging interventions were assessed for medication adherence and lifestyle management, with the SuMMiT-D study measuring attendance and adherence through blood pressure-lowering, glucose-lowering, and lipid-lowering treatment [N5-F3]. For PrEP, SMS text messaging was linked to adequate PrEP adherence [N5-R5], and telePrEP studies were evaluated for clinical and implementation outcomes [N7-R1][N7-R4]. The evidence therefore shows that digital strategies were evaluated not only on adherence but also on broader participation in care and service delivery [N5-F3][N7-R1].

Limitations and context dependence were apparent. The digital text messaging study noted that SMS systems are complex digital health interventions requiring clear theoretical underpinning and thoughtful message design [N5-F3]. It also emphasized that appraisal of the system was influenced by existing routines, lifestyle disruption, and users’ understanding of the condition [N5-F3]. For telePrEP, the evidence base is still evolving, and the systematic review highlights the need to summarize implementation and equity outcomes [N7-R1][N7-R4]. The review also notes that telePrEP may be useful but is not universally scalable across all settings [N7-R1]. In other words, digital strategies worked best when they were context-sensitive, designed with user needs in mind, and adapted to the logistics of the setting [N5-F3][N7-R1].

Overall, the evidence supports digital and remote support strategies as practical tools for retention, especially SMS and telePrEP, but these strategies were often evaluated in ways that showed they were context-dependent and required careful design rather than being universally easy to scale [N5-F3][N7-R1].

Barriers and mediators affecting retention in PrEP studies were identified across multiple levels. Major barriers included stigma, transportation, cost, and substance use. The scoping review on YMSM found that financial burdens, interpersonal stigma, and behavioral factors were significant barriers [N6-F4]. The nurse journal article listed barriers such as younger age, lower education levels, unstable housing, stigma, complicated work schedules, and lack of insurance [N6-R2]. The NACHC guide also emphasized identifying patients at risk of dropping out and using objective adherence testing to detect early attrition [N6-R4]. These sources together show that barriers were not limited to one domain: they spanned individual, social, economic, and logistical factors.

Mediators that improved retention included self-efficacy, social support, and provider engagement. The YMSM scoping review highlighted psychological strategies, supportive health systems, and supportive social networks as key facilitators [N6-F4]. ## What retention strategies have health services providing PrEP utilized according to the included studies?

Health services providing PrEP have used a broad set of retention strategies, combining counseling, linkage to care, peer navigation, reminder/remediation systems, and digital/remote support. The evidence also shows that these strategies were often embedded in clinic-based, home-based, telehealth, or hybrid delivery models, and that interventions varied in whether they were integrated into routine care or stood alone [N1-F1][N3-F2][N7-R1][N7-R5].

### 1) Core retention strategies used by health services

The core retention strategies most consistently reported in the evidence were counseling, linkage to care, peer navigation, and reminder/remediation systems.

- **Counseling** was central to routine care. One source notes that clinicians should provide medication adherence counseling and behavioral risk reduction support in conjunction with HIV-related services [N1-R4]. The systematic review of PrEP interventions also identified individual counseling as one of the Best Practices [N1-F1]. In a patient-centered combination intervention, counseling was adapted from prior PrEP studies and paired with participant-selected adherence support [N3-F2].
  
- **Linkage to care** was a major strategy for retention in the care cascade. The evidence explicitly included linkage/retention/re-engagement in HIV care as one of the topic areas in the systematic review’s cumulative database [N1-F1]. The abstract notes that linkage to PrEP care was among the most commonly reported outcomes [N1-R1]. In practice, services combined linkage with retention, as seen in the PATH-PrEP study, which involved linkage to care and HIV/STI testing as part of a broader prevention package [N4-R3].

- **Peer navigation** was another retained strategy. The systematic review cited integrated medical care with a PrEP peer navigator as one of the Best Practices [N1-F1]. Another source emphasized the crucial role of PrEP navigators in facilitating access to HIV prevention services [N2-R2]. This shows peer navigation was used to support access and retention rather than being an afterthought.

- **Reminder/remediation systems** were used to keep people engaged. The systematic review noted that digital health interventions and two-way messaging may help participants feel supported [N1-F1]. In a separate text-messaging study, SMS was described as a low-cost approach to support medication adherence and lifestyle management [N5-F3]. The evidence also indicates that services used follow-up visits and objective adherence testing to identify patients at risk of dropping out [N6-R4]. That is, retention was not only about starting PrEP, but also about monitoring and remediation.

### 2) How services structured delivery: clinic-based, home-based, telehealth, and hybrid models

The evidence shows that services did not use a single delivery model; instead, they used clinic-based, home-based, telehealth, and hybrid models.

- **Clinic-based delivery** was the most common baseline model. The systematic review identified clinic-based delivery as a core part of the field and included linkage/retention/re-engagement in HIV care among its topic areas [N1-F1]. The Malawi pilot study was delivered through antenatal and postnatal platforms, illustrating clinic-based integration into maternal health services [N3-F2]. The PATH-PrEP study also combined behavioral components with linkage to care in a clinic-based context [N4-R3].

- **Home-based delivery** emerged as a separate model for populations where in-person access was challenging. One study assessed the acceptability and feasibility of a home-based PrEP program [N7-R5]. This suggests that home-based delivery was used to reach people who might otherwise be difficult to serve, and that feasibility was a key concern in implementation [N7-R5].

- **Telehealth/telePrEP** was another major delivery model. The evidence includes a systematic review of telePrEP programs in the U.S. and a CDC report evaluating the effect of telePrEP on delivery of PrEP services at the Denver Sexual Health Clinic [N7-R1][N7-R2]. These sources show that telehealth was used as a remote delivery model and that it was studied for clinical, implementation, and equity outcomes [N7-R1][N7-R4]. The HHS report also suggested a virtual service delivery model for PrEP that could be leveraged in public health emergencies [N7-R3]. This indicates that telehealth was not only a convenience tool, but also a strategic response to service delivery constraints.

- **Hybrid models** were also evident. The PATH-PrEP study combined behavioral and linkage-to-care components [N4-R3], while the Malawi study combined patient-centered counseling and adherence support within maternal health services [N3-F2]. The telePrEP evidence also implies hybrid models because it describes telePrEP programs and their implementation outcomes, which suggests integration with existing clinic services [N7-R1][N7-R4].

### 3) Whether strategies were integrated into routine care or stand-alone interventions

The evidence suggests a spectrum from integrated routine care to stand-alone interventions.

- **Integrated into routine care** were counseling, peer navigation, and monitoring/remediation. For example, counseling was part of standard care in the systematic review [N1-F1][N3-F2], and routine follow-up visits and objective adherence testing were used to identify at-risk patients [N6-R4]. The Malawi study was delivered through antenatal and postnatal platforms, showing integration into maternal health services [N3-F2].

- **Stand-alone interventions** included digital tools and some remote support systems. Text messaging and SMS-based interventions were described as digital tools to support adherence and self-management [N5-F3][N5-R2]. The systematic review also noted that digital health interventions were among the Best Practices, but the evidence base is still limited for some populations [N1-F1].

In other words, the evidence supports a mixed approach: many interventions were embedded in routine care, while digital and remote support were often stand-alone or hybrid tools designed to reinforce adherence and retention [N1-F1][N3-F2][N5-F3].

### 4) Behavioral and patient-centered retention strategies

Behavioral and patient-centered strategies were tested and tailored to individual needs.

- **Motivational interviewing** was explicitly identified as one tested approach. The systematic review noted that individual counseling and motivational interviewing were among the Best Practices [N1-F1]. The Malawi study used patient-centered counseling adapted from prior PrEP studies [N3-F2], suggesting that motivational interviewing or similar counseling approaches were used as a core method to support adherence and retention.

- **Goal-setting and routine-building** were also part of behavioral strategies. The YMSM scoping review highlighted an established daily routine, the use of PrEP reminders, and social support as effective facilitators [N6-F4]. The NACHC guide recommended adherence counseling and behavioral risk reduction support, which implies a structured approach to behavioral change [N1-R4]. The Malawi pilot study used a structured schedule with multiple follow-up visits [N3-F2], supporting the idea that behavioral strategies were implemented through regular follow-up and routine care.

- **Patient-centered features** that improved adherence included preferences, confidentiality, and navigator support. The Malawi study allowed participants to select an adherence supporter, showing that preferences were central to the intervention design [N3-F2]. The NACHC guide emphasized confidentiality and behavioral risk reduction support [N1-R4]. The scoping review also noted supportive health systems and supportive social networks as effective facilitators [N6-F4], indicating that social support and supportive environments were part of the patient-centered package.

- **Implementation in real-world PrEP services** was varied. The Malawi study was integrated into antenatal and postnatal services [N3-F2], while the PATH-PrEP study combined behavioral and linkage-to-care components [N4-R3]. The best-practice review also noted that digital health interventions and peer navigation were among the Best Practices, showing that behavioral strategies were adapted across settings and delivery models [N1-F1]. Overall, behavioral strategies were not isolated interventions; they were implemented as part of routine care, combined with counseling, peer support, and structured follow-up [N1-F1][N3-F2][N4-R3].

### 5) Digital and remote support strategies

Digital and remote support strategies were centered on text messaging, telehealth, and digital messaging systems.

- **Text messaging** was the most frequently cited tool. Studies described SMS-based interventions, text-messaging applications, and ecological momentary intervention systems [N5-R1][N5-R3]. The evidence also explicitly links text messaging to medication adherence and lifestyle management [N5-F3]. For PrEP, SMS text messaging improved adequate PrEP adherence among young MSM [N5-R5], and an interactive text-messaging intervention improved adherence among young MSM in Chicago [N5-R2].

- **Telehealth/telePrEP** was another major digital support model. The evidence includes a systematic review of telePrEP programs in the U.S., which aimed to describe model characteristics and summarize clinical, implementation, and equity outcomes [N7-R1][N7-R4]. A CDC report evaluated the effect of telePrEP on delivery of PrEP services at the Denver Sexual Health Clinic [N7-R2]. These sources indicate that telehealth was used as a remote delivery model and that it was positioned as a scalable and flexible option for service delivery [N7-R1][N7-R3].

- **Retention outcomes measured** included adherence and appointment attendance. Text messaging interventions were assessed for medication adherence and lifestyle management [N5-F3]. For PrEP, SMS text messaging was linked to adequate adherence [N5-R5]. TelePrEP studies were evaluated for clinical and implementation outcomes [N7-R1][N7-R4]. So the evidence shows that digital strategies were evaluated not only on adherence but also on broader participation in care and service delivery [N5-F3][N7-R1].

- **Limitations and context dependence** were apparent. The digital text messaging study noted that SMS systems are complex digital health interventions requiring clear theoretical underpinning and thoughtful message design [N5-F3]. It also emphasized that appraisal of the system was influenced by existing routines, lifestyle disruption, and users’ understanding of the condition [N5-F3]. For telePrEP, the evidence base is still evolving, and the systematic review highlights the need to summarize implementation and equity outcomes [N7-R1][N7-R4]. The review also notes that telePrEP may be useful but is not universally scalable across all settings [N7-R1]. In short, digital strategies worked best when they were context-sensitive, designed with user needs in mind, and adapted to the logistics of the setting [N5-F3][N7-R1].

### 6) Barriers and mediators that affect retention

Barriers and mediators affected retention across multiple levels.

- **Major barriers** included stigma, transportation, cost, and substance use. The scoping review on YMSM found that financial burdens, interpersonal stigma, and behavioral factors were significant barriers [N6-F4]. The nurse journal article listed barriers such as younger age, lower education levels, unstable housing, stigma, complicated work schedules, and lack of insurance [N6-R2]. The NACHC guide also emphasized identifying patients at risk of dropping out and using objective adherence testing to detect early attrition [N6-R4]. These sources together show that barriers were not limited to one domain: they spanned individual, social, economic, and logistical factors.

- **Mediators** that improved retention included self-efficacy, social support, and provider engagement. The YMSM scoping review highlighted psychological strategies, supportive health systems, and supportive social networks as key facilitators [N6-F4]. It also noted that effective facilitators included an established daily routine, PrEP reminders, and social support [N6-F4]. The NACHC guide emphasized provider counseling and behavioral risk reduction support as part of routine care [N1-R4], which is consistent with provider engagement as a mediator. Together, these sources suggest that retention was more likely when individuals felt supported by their social networks, had a routine, and had engaged providers [N6-F4][N1-R4].

- **How barriers and mediators were measured** varied by study design. The scoping review synthesized qualitative findings and used meta-synthesis to interpret barriers and facilitators across 14 studies [N6-F4]. The nurse journal article listed barriers without detailed measurement methods, so its evidence is descriptive rather than methodologically detailed [N6-R2]. The NACHC guide provided practical implementation guidance, including objective adherence testing and follow-up visits, which indicates that barriers were addressed through monitoring and remediation [N6-R4]. In other words, some studies measured barriers through qualitative synthesis, while others used observational indicators such as retention and adherence testing [N6-F4][N6-R4].

- **Whether interventions addressed these barriers and mediators** is clear. The Best Practices review noted that digital health interventions and peer navigator models were among the best practices, implying that interventions were designed to counter barriers such as stigma, complexity, and poor access [N1-F1]. The YMSM scoping review emphasized tailored, multi-level interventions and healthcare provider training in youth-specific approaches [N6-F4]. These examples show that the evidence base is not only descriptive but also intervention-oriented: the same barriers were addressed through digital tools, peer support, routine counseling, and system-level changes [N1-F1][N6-F4][N6-R4].

### 7) Role of implementation context and delivery models

Implementation context and delivery models shaped the effectiveness of retention strategies.

- **Delivery models studied** included clinic-based, home-based, telehealth, and hybrid models. Clinic-based delivery was the most common baseline model, and the systematic review identified it as a core part of the field [N1-F1]. Home-based delivery was assessed for acceptability and feasibility [N7-R5]. Telehealth/telePrEP was studied as a remote delivery model [N7-R1][N7-R2]. Hybrid models were also evident, as seen in the PATH-PrEP study and the Malawi study [N4-R3][N3-F2].

- **Context influenced effectiveness** in several ways. Setting mattered because interventions were adapted to maternal and child health platforms, home-based care, and telehealth environments [N3-F2][N7-R5][N7-R1]. Provider role mattered because the evidence included peer navigators, motivational interviewing, and integrated medical care [N1-F1][N3-F2]. Logistics mattered because telePrEP was evaluated for its effect on service delivery, and home-based delivery was assessed for acceptability and feasibility [N7-R2][N7-R5]. Overall, the evidence shows that delivery models were shaped by context, and effectiveness depended on how well the model fit the setting, the provider role, and the logistics of the population being served [N1-F1][N3-F2][N7-R1].

### 8) Bottom line

The included studies show that health services providing PrEP have used a combination of strategies to improve retention. The most common interventions were counseling, linkage to care, peer navigation, and reminder/remediation systems [N1-F1][N1-R4][N2-R2][N6-R4]. These were often embedded in routine care, especially clinic-based delivery, but also extended to home-based and telehealth models [N3-F2][N7-R5][N7-R1]. Digital and remote support strategies, particularly text messaging and telePrEP, were increasingly used as tools to reinforce adherence and attendance [N5-F3][N5-R5][N7-R1]. Behavioral and patient-centered strategies, including motivational interviewing, goal-setting, and preferences-based support, were tested to improve adherence through routine care and structured follow-up [N1-F1][N6-F4][N3-F2]. Finally, barriers such as stigma, cost, and substance use were recognized, while mediators such as social support and provider engagement were shown to improve retention [N6-F4][N1-R4].

In short, the evidence supports a mixed, context-sensitive approach to PrEP retention: integrate counseling and peer support into routine care, use linkage and navigation to keep people engaged, and supplement with digital tools and hybrid delivery models when appropriate [N1-F1][N3-F2][N7-R1].

The evidence includes a systematic review of telePrEP programs in the U.S., which aimed to describe model characteristics and summarize clinical, implementation, and equity outcomes [N7-R1][N7-R4]. A CDC report also evaluated the effect of telePrEP on delivery of PrEP services at the Denver Sexual Health Clinic [N7-R2]. These sources indicate that telehealth was used as a remote delivery model rather than a one-off tool, and that it was positioned as a scalable and flexible option for service delivery [N7-R1]. Barriers and mediators affecting retention in PrEP studies were identified across multiple levels. Major barriers included stigma, transportation, cost, and substance use. The scoping review on YMSM found that financial burdens, interpersonal stigma, and behavioral factors were significant barriers [N6-F4]. The nurse journal article listed barriers such as younger age, lower education levels, unstable housing, stigma, complicated work schedules, and lack of insurance [N6-R2]. The NACHC guide also emphasized identifying patients at risk of dropping out and using objective adherence testing to detect early attrition [N6-R4]. These sources together show that barriers were not limited to one domain: they spanned individual, social, economic, and logistical factors.

Mediators that improved retention included self-efficacy, social support, and provider engagement. The YMSM scoping review highlighted psychological strategies, supportive health systems, and supportive social networks as key facilitators [N6-F4]. It also noted that effective facilitators included an established daily routine, PrEP reminders, and social support [N6-F4]. The NACHC guide emphasized provider counseling and behavioral risk reduction support as part of routine care [N1-R4], which is consistent with provider engagement as a mediator. Together, these sources suggest that retention was more likely when individuals felt supported by their social networks, had a routine, and had engaged providers [N6-F4][N1-R4].

How barriers and mediators were measured varied by study design. The scoping review synthesized qualitative findings and used meta-synthesis to interpret barriers and facilitators across 14 studies [N6-F4]. The nurse journal article listed barriers without detailed measurement methods, so its evidence is descriptive rather than methodologically detailed [N6-R2]. The NACHC guide provided practical implementation guidance, including objective adherence testing and follow-up visits, which indicates that barriers were addressed through monitoring and remediation [N6-R4]. In other words, some studies measured barriers through qualitative synthesis, while others used observational indicators such as retention and adherence testing [N6-F4][N6-R4].

The evidence also shows that interventions addressed these barriers and mediators directly. The Best Practices review noted that digital health interventions and peer navigator models were among the best practices, implying that interventions were designed to counter barriers such as stigma, complexity, and poor access [N1-F1]. The YMSM scoping review emphasized tailored, multi-level interventions and healthcare provider training in youth-specific approaches [N6-F4]. These examples show that the evidence base is not only descriptive but also intervention-oriented: the same barriers were addressed through digital tools, peer support, routine counseling, and system-level changes [N1-F1][N6-F4][N6-R4].

### 3) Whether strategies were integrated into routine care or stand-alone interventions

The evidence suggests a spectrum from integrated routine care to stand-alone interventions.

The Malawi study was delivered through antenatal and postnatal platforms, showing integration into maternal health services [N3-F2].

Text messaging and SMS-based interventions were described as digital tools to support adherence and self-management [N5-F3][N5-R2]. The systematic review also noted that digital health interventions were among the Best Practices, but the evidence base is still limited for some populations [N1-F1].

In other words, the evidence supports a mixed approach: many interventions were embedded in routine care, while digital and remote support were often stand-alone or hybrid tools designed to reinforce adherence and retention [N1-F1][N3-F2][N5-F3].

### 4) Behavioral and patient-centered retention strategies

Behavioral and patient-centered strategies were tested and tailored to individual needs.

- **Motivational interviewing** was explicitly identified as one tested approach. The systematic review noted that individual counseling and motivational interviewing were among the Best Practices [N1-F1]. The Malawi study used patient-centered counseling adapted from prior PrEP studies [N3-F2], suggesting that motivational interviewing or similar counseling approaches were used as a core method to support adherence and retention.

- **Goal-setting and routine-building** were also part of behavioral strategies. The YMSM scoping review highlighted an established daily routine, the use of PrEP reminders, and social support as effective facilitators [N6-F4]. The NACHC guide recommended adherence counseling and behavioral risk reduction support, which implies a structured approach to behavioral change [N1-R4]. The Malawi pilot study used a structured schedule with multiple follow-up visits [N3-F2], supporting the idea that behavioral strategies were implemented through regular follow-up and routine care.

- **Patient-centered features** that improved adherence included preferences, confidentiality, and navigator support. The Malawi study allowed participants to select an adherence supporter, showing that preferences were central to the intervention design [N3-F2]. The NACHC guide emphasized confidentiality and behavioral risk reduction support [N1-R4]. The scoping review also noted supportive health systems and supportive social networks as effective facilitators [N6-F4], indicating that social support and supportive environments were part of the patient-centered package.

- **Implementation in real-world PrEP services** was varied. The Malawi study was integrated into antenatal and postnatal services [N3-F2], while the PATH-PrEP study combined behavioral and linkage-to-care components [N4-R3]. The best-practice review also noted that digital health interventions and peer navigation were among the Best Practices, showing that behavioral strategies were adapted across settings and delivery models [N1-F1]. Overall, behavioral strategies were not isolated interventions; they were implemented as part of routine care, combined with counseling, peer support, and structured follow-up [N1-F1][N3-F2][N4-R3].

### 5) Digital and remote support strategies

Digital and remote support strategies were centered on text messaging, telehealth, and digital messaging systems.

- **Text messaging** was the most frequently cited tool. Studies described SMS-based interventions, text-messaging applications, and ecological momentary intervention systems [N5-R1][N5-R3]. The evidence also explicitly links text messaging to medication adherence and lifestyle management [N5-F3]. - **Telehealth/telePrEP** was another major digital support model. - **Retention outcomes measured** included adherence and appointment attendance. Text messaging interventions were assessed for medication adherence and lifestyle management [N5-F3]. For PrEP, SMS text messaging was linked to adequate adherence [N5-R5]. TelePrEP studies were evaluated for clinical and implementation outcomes [N7-R1][N7-R4]. - **Limitations and context dependence** were apparent. The digital text messaging study noted that SMS systems are complex digital health interventions requiring clear theoretical underpinning and thoughtful message design [N5-F3]. It also emphasized that appraisal of the system was influenced by existing routines, lifestyle disruption, and users’ understanding of the condition [N5-F3]. The review also notes that telePrEP may be useful but is not universally scalable across all settings [N7-R1]. In short, digital strategies worked best when they were context-sensitive, designed with user needs in mind, and adapted to the logistics of the setting [N5-F3][N7-R1].

### 6) Barriers and mediators that affect retention

Barriers and mediators affected retention across multiple levels.

- **Major barriers** included stigma, transportation, cost, and substance use. The scoping review on YMSM found that financial burdens, interpersonal stigma, and behavioral factors were significant barriers [N6-F4]. The nurse journal article listed barriers such as younger age, lower education levels, unstable housing, stigma, complicated work schedules, and lack of insurance [N6-R2]. The NACHC guide also emphasized identifying patients at risk of dropping out and using objective adherence testing to detect early attrition [N6-R4]. These sources together show that barriers were not limited to one domain: they spanned individual, social, economic, and logistical factors.

- **Mediators** that improved retention included self-efficacy, social support, and provider engagement. The YMSM scoping review highlighted psychological strategies, supportive health systems, and supportive social networks as key facilitators [N6-F4]. It also noted that effective facilitators included an established daily routine, PrEP reminders, and social support [N6-F4]. The NACHC guide emphasized provider counseling and behavioral risk reduction support as part of routine care [N1-R4], which is consistent with provider engagement as a mediator. Together, these sources suggest that retention was more likely when individuals felt supported by their social networks, had a routine, and had engaged providers [N6-F4][N1-R4].

- **How barriers and mediators were measured** varied by study design. The scoping review synthesized qualitative findings and used meta-synthesis to interpret barriers and facilitators across 14 studies [N6-F4]. The nurse journal article listed barriers without detailed measurement methods, so its evidence is descriptive rather than methodologically detailed [N6-R2]. The NACHC guide provided practical implementation guidance, including objective adherence testing and follow-up visits, which indicates that barriers were addressed through monitoring and remediation [N6-R4]. In other words, some studies measured barriers through qualitative synthesis, while others used observational indicators such as retention and adherence testing [N6-F4][N6-R4].

- **Whether interventions addressed these barriers and mediators** is clear. The Best Practices review noted that digital health interventions and peer navigator models were among the best practices, implying that interventions were designed to counter barriers such as stigma, complexity, and poor access [N1-F1]. The YMSM scoping review emphasized tailored, multi-level interventions and healthcare provider training in youth-specific approaches [N6-F4]. These examples show that the evidence base is not only descriptive but also intervention-oriented: the same barriers were addressed through digital tools, peer support, routine counseling, and system-level changes [N1-F1][N6-F4][N6-R4].

### 7) Role of implementation context and delivery models

Implementation context and delivery models shaped the effectiveness of retention strategies.

- **Delivery models studied** included clinic-based, home-based, telehealth, and hybrid models. Clinic-based delivery was the most common baseline model, and the systematic review identified it as a core part of the field [N1-F1]. Home-based delivery was assessed for acceptability and feasibility [N7-R5]. Telehealth/telePrEP was studied as a remote delivery model [N7-R1][N7-R2]. Hybrid models were also evident, as seen in the PATH-PrEP study and the Malawi study [N4-R3][N3-F2].

- **Context influenced effectiveness** in several ways. Setting mattered because interventions were adapted to maternal and child health platforms, home-based care, and telehealth environments [N3-F2][N7-R5][N7-R1]. Provider role mattered because the evidence included peer navigators, motivational interviewing, and integrated medical care [N1-F1][N3-F2]. Logistics mattered because telePrEP was evaluated for its effect on service delivery, and home-based delivery was assessed for acceptability and feasibility [N7-R2][N7-R5]. Overall, the evidence shows that delivery models were shaped by context, and effectiveness depended on how well the model fit the setting, the provider role, and the logistics of the population being served [N1-F1][N3-F2][N7-R1].

### 8) Bottom line

The included studies show that health services providing PrEP have used a combination of strategies to improve retention. The most common interventions were counseling, linkage to care, peer navigation, and reminder/remediation systems [N1-F1][N1-R4][N2-R2][N6-R4]. These were often embedded in routine care, especially clinic-based delivery, but also extended to home-based and telehealth models [N3-F2][N7-R5][N7-R1]. Digital and remote support strategies, particularly text messaging and telePrEP, were increasingly used as tools to reinforce adherence and attendance [N5-F3][N5-R5][N7-R1]. Behavioral and patient-centered strategies, including motivational interviewing, goal-setting, and preferences-based support, were tested to improve adherence through routine care and structured follow-up [N1-F1][N6-F4][N3-F2]. Finally, barriers such as stigma, cost, and substance use were recognized, while mediators such as social support and provider engagement were shown to improve retention [N6-F4][N1-R4].

In short, the evidence supports a mixed, context-sensitive approach to PrEP retention: integrate counseling and peer support into routine care, use linkage and navigation to keep people engaged, and supplement with digital tools and hybrid delivery models when appropriate [N1-F1][N3-F2][N7-R1].

Core retention strategies used by health services in PrEP studies were broad and often combined counseling, linkage to care, peer navigation, and reminder/remediation systems. The evidence suggests that counseling was central to routine care, with one review noting that clinicians should provide medication adherence counseling and behavioral risk reduction support in conjunction with HIV-related services [N1-R4]. A systematic review also found that among 26 eligible interventions, nine met Best Practices, including individual counseling, motivational interviewing, integrated medical care with a PrEP peer navigator, and digital health interventions [N1-F1]. In another setting, a patient-centered combination intervention included patient-centered counseling adapted from prior PrEP studies plus the option of a participant-selected adherence supporter [N3-F2]. These examples show that counseling was not a stand-alone gimmick but was integrated into service delivery and tailored to participants’ preferences.

Linkage to care was also a major strategy, especially for retention in the care cascade. The systematic review explicitly included linkage/retention/re-engagement in HIV care as one of the five topic areas in its cumulative database [N1-F1], and the abstract notes that linkage to PrEP care was among the most commonly reported outcomes [N1-R1]. In practice, services combined linkage with retention; for example, the PATH-PrEP study involved linkage to care and HIV/STI testing as part of a broader prevention package [N4-R3]. The evidence also points to peer navigation as a retained strategy: the systematic review cited integrated medical care with a PrEP peer navigator as one of the Best Practices [N1-F1], and another study emphasized the crucial role of PrEP navigators in facilitating access to HIV prevention services [N2-R2]. So peer navigation was used to support access and retention rather than being an afterthought.

Reminder systems were similarly embedded in routine care. The systematic review identified digital health interventions and noted that two-way messaging may help participants feel supported [N1-F1]. In a separate text-messaging intervention study, SMS was described as a low-cost approach to support medication adherence and lifestyle management, with messages designed to affect self-management and behavior change [N5-F3]. Though this is not a PrEP-specific study, its evidence base is directly relevant here because it illustrates how reminder-based digital support was used in health services. The evidence also indicates that services used follow-up visits and objective adherence testing to identify patients at risk of dropping out [N6-R4]. That is, health services did not rely on a single intervention; they used monitoring and remediation to keep people engaged.

Delivery models were varied and often mixed. Clinic-based delivery was clearly the baseline model, especially for integrated care and standard counseling [N1-F1][N3-F2]. Home-based delivery emerged as a separate model, with one study assessing the acceptability and feasibility of a home-based PrEP program [N7-R5]. Telehealth/telePrEP was another major model, with systematic reviews and reports describing virtual service delivery, telePrEP programs, and the effects of telePrEP on service delivery [N7-R1][N7-R3]. The evidence also points to hybrid models: the PATH-PrEP study combined behavioral and linkage-to-care components [N4-R3], and the Malawi pilot study was delivered through antenatal and postnatal platforms [N3-F2]. So delivery models were not fixed; they were adapted to the setting, and many studies used combinations of clinic visits, home-based support, and telehealth.

Whether strategies were integrated or stand-alone depended on the intervention design. Counseling and peer navigation were often integrated into routine care, such as in standard counseling and integrated medical care [N1-F1][N3-F2]. Digital interventions, by contrast, were sometimes stand-alone in their design, such as SMS-based interventions [N5-R2][N5-R5]. The review also emphasized that digital health interventions may be highly scalable, but the evidence base is still limited for some populations [N1-F1]. In short, the evidence supports a spectrum from routine clinic-based care with counseling and peer support, through home-based and telehealth models, to digital reminder systems and hybrid programs [N1-F1][N3-F2][N7-R1].

Digital and remote support strategies in the evidence were centered on text messaging, telehealth, and digital messaging systems. Text messaging was the most frequently cited tool, with studies describing SMS-based interventions, text-messaging applications, and ecological momentary intervention systems [N5-R1][N5-R3]. The evidence also explicitly links text messaging to medication adherence support and self-management [N5-F3]. In PrEP-specific studies, SMS text messaging improved adequate PrEP adherence among young MSM [N5-R5], and an interactive text-messaging intervention improved adherence among young MSM in Chicago [N5-R2]. The digital text messaging intervention was therefore used as a stand-alone support strategy to reinforce adherence and retention.

Telehealth/telePrEP was another major digital support model. The evidence includes a systematic review of telePrEP programs in the U.S., which aimed to describe model characteristics and summarize clinical, implementation, and equity outcomes [N7-R1][N7-R4]. A CDC report also evaluated the effect of telePrEP on delivery of PrEP services at the Denver Sexual Health Clinic [N7-R2]. These sources indicate that telehealth was used as a remote delivery model rather than a one-off tool, and that it was positioned as a scalable and flexible option for service delivery [N7-R1]. The evidence further suggests that telehealth can be leveraged in public health emergencies, such as during the pandemic, which reinforces its remote support function [N7-R3].

Retention outcomes measured in these studies included adherence and appointment attendance. Text messaging interventions were assessed for medication adherence and lifestyle management, with the SuMMiT-D study measuring attendance and adherence through blood pressure-lowering, glucose-lowering, and lipid-lowering treatment [N5-F3]. For PrEP, SMS text messaging was linked to adequate PrEP adherence [N5-R5], and telePrEP studies were evaluated for clinical and implementation outcomes [N7-R1][N7-R4]. The evidence therefore shows that digital strategies were evaluated not only on adherence but also on broader participation in care and service delivery [N5-F3][N7-R1].

Limitations and context dependence were apparent. The digital text messaging study noted that SMS systems are complex digital health interventions requiring clear theoretical underpinning and thoughtful message design [N5-F3]. It also emphasized that appraisal of the system was influenced by existing routines, lifestyle disruption, and users’ understanding of the condition [N5-F3]. For telePrEP, the evidence base is still evolving, and the systematic review highlights the need to summarize implementation and equity outcomes [N7-R1][N7-R4]. The review also notes that telePrEP may be useful but is not universally scalable across all settings [N7-R1]. In other words, digital strategies worked best when they were context-sensitive, designed with user needs in mind, and adapted to the logistics of the setting [N5-F3][N7-R1].

Overall, the evidence supports digital and remote support strategies as practical tools for retention, especially SMS and telePrEP, but these strategies were often evaluated in ways that showed they were context-dependent and required careful design rather than being universally easy to scale [N5-F3][N7-R1].

Barriers and mediators affecting retention in PrEP studies were identified across multiple levels. Major barriers included stigma, transportation, cost, and substance use. The scoping review on YMSM found that financial burdens, interpersonal stigma, and behavioral factors were significant barriers [N6-F4]. The nurse journal article listed barriers such as younger age, lower education levels, unstable housing, stigma, complicated work schedules, and lack of insurance [N6-R2]. The NACHC guide also emphasized identifying patients at risk of dropping out and using objective adherence testing to detect early attrition [N6-R4]. These sources together show that barriers were not limited to one domain: they spanned individual, social, economic, and logistical factors.

Mediators that improved retention included self-efficacy, social support, and provider engagement. The YMSM scoping review highlighted psychological strategies, supportive health systems, and supportive social networks as key facilitators [N6-F4]. It also noted that effective facilitators included an established daily routine, PrEP reminders, and social support [N6-F4]. The NACHC guide emphasized provider counseling and behavioral risk reduction support as part of routine care [N1-R4], which is consistent with provider engagement as a mediator. Together, these sources suggest that retention was more likely when individuals felt supported by their social networks, had a routine, and had engaged providers [N6-F4][N1-R4].

How barriers and mediators were measured varied by study design. The scoping review synthesized qualitative findings and used meta-synthesis to interpret barriers and facilitators across 14 studies [N6-F4]. The nurse journal article listed barriers without detailed measurement methods, so its evidence is descriptive rather than methodologically detailed [N6-R2]. The NACHC guide provided practical implementation guidance, including objective adherence testing and follow-up visits, which indicates that barriers were addressed through monitoring and remediation [N6-R4]. In other words, some studies measured barriers through qualitative synthesis, while others used observational indicators such as retention and adherence testing [N6-F4][N6-R4].

The evidence also shows that interventions addressed these barriers and mediators directly. The Best Practices review noted that digital health interventions and peer navigator models were among the best practices, implying that interventions were designed to counter barriers such as stigma, complexity, and poor access [N1-F1]. The YMSM scoping review emphasized tailored, multi-level interventions and healthcare provider training in youth-specific approaches [N6-F4]. These examples show that the evidence base is not only descriptive but also intervention-oriented: the same barriers were addressed through digital tools, peer support, routine counseling, and system-level changes [N1-F1][N6-F4][N6-R4].

- **Delivery models studied** included clinic-based, home-based, telehealth, and hybrid models. Clinic-based delivery was the most common baseline model, and the systematic review identified it as a core part of the field [N1-F1]. Home-based delivery was assessed for acceptability and feasibility [N7-R5]. Telehealth/telePrEP was studied as a remote delivery model [N7-R1][N7-R2]. Hybrid models were also evident, as seen in the PATH-PrEP study and the Malawi study [N4-R3][N3-F2].

- **Context influenced effectiveness** in several ways. Setting mattered because interventions were adapted to maternal and child health platforms, home-based care, and telehealth environments [N3-F2][N7-R5][N7-R1]. Provider role mattered because the evidence included peer navigators, motivational interviewing, and integrated medical care [N1-F1][N3-F2]. Logistics mattered because telePrEP was evaluated for its effect on service delivery, and home-based delivery was assessed for acceptability and feasibility [N7-R2][N7-R5]. Overall, the evidence shows that delivery models were shaped by context, and effectiveness depended on how well the model fit the setting, the provider role, and the logistics of the population being served [N1-F1][N3-F2][N7-R1].

### 8) Bottom line

The included studies show that health services providing PrEP have used a combination of strategies to improve retention. The most common interventions were counseling, linkage to care, peer navigation, and reminder/remediation systems [N1-F1][N1-R4][N2-R2][N6-R4]. These were often embedded in routine care, especially clinic-based delivery, but also extended to home-based and telehealth models [N3-F2][N7-R5][N7-R1]. Digital and remote support strategies, particularly text messaging and telePrEP, were increasingly used as tools to reinforce adherence and attendance [N5-F3][N5-R5][N7-R1]. Behavioral and patient-centered strategies, including motivational interviewing, goal-setting, and preferences-based support, were tested to improve adherence through routine care and structured follow-up [N1-F1][N6-F4][N3-F2]. Finally, barriers such as stigma, cost, and substance use were recognized, while mediators such as social support and provider engagement were shown to improve retention [N6-F4][N1-R4].

In short, the evidence supports a mixed, context-sensitive approach to PrEP retention: integrate counseling and peer support into routine care, use linkage and navigation to keep people engaged, and supplement with digital tools and hybrid delivery models when appropriate [N1-F1][N3-F2][N7-R1].
